name: Qing Dynasty
line: Rise early, practise your brush, study one book through and keep a diary.

quote.text: The rise and fall of all under heaven is the responsibility of every ordinary person.
quote.source: The eight-character saying drawn from his Record of Daily Knowledge, about 1670, in the form given it by Liang Qichao

quotes.text: Esteem most highly filial piety and brotherly submission, in order to give due importance to human moral relations.
quotes.source: The first of the sixteen maxims of the Sacred Edict, 1670, read aloud in every village twice a month

quotes.text: Truth becomes fiction when the fiction’s true; real becomes not-real where the unreal’s real.
quotes.source: The couplet on the gateway to the Land of Illusion; The Story of the Stone, chapter 1, trans. David Hawkes

quotes.text: The sea accepts a hundred rivers; its greatness lies in its capacity.
quotes.source: The first line of a couplet he wrote for his office in Guangzhou, 1839

quotes.text: I set no value on objects strange or ingenious, and have no use for your country’s manufactures.
quotes.source: Edict to King George III, 1793, trans. E. Backhouse and J. O. P. Bland

quotes.text: Pages full of idle words, penned with hot and bitter tears.
quotes.source: The Story of the Stone, chapter 1, trans. David Hawkes

quotes.text: Do not ask about the harvest. Ask only about the ploughing.
quotes.source: A maxim from his diaries and family letters, as commonly cited

words.usage: The name the Manchu rulers gave their dynasty in 1636. Its character contains the sign for water.
The civilised world as the court understood it: an order centred on the emperor, with no fixed outer edge.
The right to rule, granted by heaven to the virtuous and withdrawn from the unworthy. Floods and rebellions were read as warnings.
The Son of Heaven. Qing emperors rose before dawn and read and answered reports in red ink for hours each day.
The Purple Forbidden City: the walled palace in the centre of Beijing, home to twenty-four emperors.
The people from north-east of the Great Wall who founded the dynasty. They were perhaps two per cent of the empire’s population.
The hereditary military and social units into which all Manchus, and allied Mongols and Chinese, were enrolled.
The ladder of written tests on the classics by which officials were chosen. Open in principle to almost any man.
Holder of the highest degree, won in the palace examination. About three hundred were made every three years.
The rigid form required in the examinations: eight sections in balanced, parallel prose on a line from the classics.
Degree holders and retired officials, who ran local affairs between the magistrate and the people.
The cultivated amateur who writes poems, paints, practises calligraphy and collects, whether or not he holds office.
The method of writing. The first of the arts, and a daily discipline held to reveal a person’s character.

words.meaning: The four treasures of the study
words.usage: Brush, ink stick, paper and inkstone. A scholar’s essential tools, chosen and cherished.
The scholar’s own room. Each was given a poetic name, which its owner often used as a pen name.
The great Qing school of scholarship: seek truth from facts by close study of old texts, inscriptions and language.
A daily record. Serious men kept one as a tool of self-examination and showed it to friends for criticism.
The Confucian form of meditation: sitting upright and still to collect the mind.
Reverent care for parents and ancestors. The root of every other virtue in the official teaching.
The right form for every relation and occasion, from a state sacrifice to how one hands over a cup of tea.
The building where a lineage keeps the tablets of its forebears and meets for rites and business.
The printed record of a lineage, with its rules and its dead. Qing families compiled them in great numbers.
Four ranges of rooms round a square court, closed to the street. The house of Beijing.
The narrow alleys between Beijing’s courtyard houses. The word is Mongol in origin.
A composed landscape of rock, water, plants and pavilions, made to be walked through like a scroll.
The southern way of brewing fine tea in a tiny pot and drinking it from thimble cups. It took shape in the Qing.
One of the four accomplishments of a gentleman, with the zither, calligraphy and painting.
The quiet instrument of the scholar, played alone or for one friend.
Kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground. Three kneelings and nine knockings were owed to the emperor.
The Manchu hairstyle of shaved forehead and long plait, imposed on all Chinese men in 1645 as a sign of submission.

practices.name: Rise at dawn and sit quietly
practices.instructions: Get up at first light without lingering. Wash your face and put the room in order. Then sit upright on a chair or cushion, hands resting, eyes lowered, and be still for ten minutes. Do not try to empty the mind. Let it settle, like silt in a jar of water. When it wanders to the day’s business, bring it back to the breath and the straight spine. Then stand, and begin.
practices.why: In 1842 the young official Zeng Guofan drew up twelve rules for his own daily conduct, and these were the first three: be reverent, sit quietly for a period each day, and rise early. He held to them, with lapses he recorded, for thirty years. The Kangxi Emperor rose at five to read with his tutors before the morning audience.
variations: Sit for the time it takes one stick of incense to burn.
Keep the same rising time every day for a month.
Sit again for five minutes before bed.

practices.name: A page with the brush
practices.instructions: After breakfast, write for twenty-five minutes by hand. If you can, use a brush, ink and absorbent paper, and copy a page of a model text one character at a time, looking hard at each before you write it. If you have no brush, copy a passage you admire in your best handwriting with a good pen. Sit straight, hold the brush upright, breathe evenly and do not hurry or go back over a stroke.
practices.why: Zeng Guofan’s rule was to practise calligraphy for an hour after the morning meal. Every educated person in Qing China wrote with a brush daily and spent years copying the models of earlier masters. Handwriting was read as a portrait of character: a slack hand meant a slack mind.
variations: Grind your own ink on a stone, slowly, before you begin.
Keep the pages, date them, and compare them after thirty days.

practices.name: One book, and what you learned
practices.instructions: Choose one serious book and read it straight through this month. Do not start another until it is finished. Read for thirty minutes with a pencil in your hand. Then read ten pages of history. When you stop, write down in a notebook one thing you learned today that you did not know yesterday, with the page it came from. Once a month, look back to make sure you have not forgotten what you knew.
practices.why: Three of Zeng’s twelve rules cover this: do not open a second book before finishing the first, read ten pages of the histories daily, and record each day what you have newly learned. The last rule comes from the great scholar Gu Yanwu, who called his life’s notebook the Record of Daily Knowledge and checked every claim against the sources.
variations: Copy out one sentence worth keeping.
Check one thing you have always believed against a good source.
Tell someone what you learned today, in two sentences.

practices.name: Tea, and a turn in the garden
practices.instructions: In mid-afternoon stop work and make tea properly. Warm a small pot and cups with hot water. Use good leaf, and pour the first quick infusion away. Brew the second for a few breaths and pour it out completely. Look at the colour, smell it, and drink in three sips. Make two or three more infusions. Then walk slowly for ten minutes among plants, in a garden, a park or a courtyard, and look at one thing closely: a rock, a branch, moving water.
practices.why: The scholar’s afternoon belonged to tea, friends and the garden. Qing writers composed whole books on water and leaf, and the Qianlong Emperor carried a small silver measure to weigh the water of every spring he visited. Zeng Guofan’s rule was to walk a thousand paces after each meal.
variations: Tend a potted plant or a tray landscape.
Invite one friend, and talk of anything except work.
Play a short game of Go.

practices.name: The evening diary
practices.instructions: Before bed write the day’s entry in a bound book, in your neatest hand. Record what you did and whom you saw. Then examine yourself under three heads. Speech: did you say anything false, boastful or unkind? Conduct: where were you lazy, irritable or self-indulgent? Study: what did you learn? Write the faults down plainly. Finish with one line to your parents or elders, living or dead. Do not go out again tonight.
practices.why: Zeng Guofan kept his diary in careful standard script and filled it with reproaches to himself for sleeping late, talking too much and looking at women. He sent it to his brothers and teacher to read. His last rules were to guard his speech, to protect his health and never to go out at night.
variations: Once a month, show a page to a friend you trust and ask for criticism.
On the first and fifteenth of the month, bow to your ancestors’ names.

tasks.name: Read the first chapter of The Story of the Stone
Listen to Flowing Water on the qin, played by Guan Pinghu
Watch The Last Emperor
tasks.meta: Watch · filmed inside the Forbidden City

tasks.name: Play one game of Go on a small board
Journal: what did you newly learn today?
Is every ordinary person responsible for the state of the world?
Walk a thousand paces after each meal
Speak less today, and nothing boastful
Write a few lines of verse about what is outside your window
tasks.meta: A poem a month, at least

tasks.name: Warm the pot, rinse the leaves and pour tea in three small cups
tasks.meta: The first cup is for the nose

tasks.name: Write one character with water on a stone or the pavement
tasks.meta: It dries, and that is fine

tasks.name: Hang something for the birds and listen
Look at the moon and think of someone who can see it too

rules.why: Up at first light, every day. The morning sets the tone of the mind.
A short period of stillness to collect yourself before the world arrives.

rules.text: Finish one book before starting another
rules.why: Depth before breadth. Scattered reading leaves nothing behind.
A page of careful writing trains patience, attention and character together.
Say less. Nothing false, nothing boastful, nothing behind another’s back.

rules.text: Keep a diary and name your faults
rules.why: Write the day down honestly every night, and let someone you respect read it.

read.title: The Story of the Stone
read.creator: Cao Xueqin, trans. David Hawkes and John Minford
read.why: Also called Dream of the Red Chamber. The life and decline of a great household, with some four hundred characters. The supreme Chinese novel, and the fullest picture of Qing life.

read.title: Emperor of China: Self-Portrait of K’ang-hsi
read.creator: Jonathan D. Spence
read.why: The Kangxi Emperor in his own words, pieced together from his letters and edicts: on hunting, ruling, medicine, his sons and growing old.

read.title: Six Records of a Floating Life
read.creator: Shen Fu
read.why: A minor clerk remembers his marriage to a woman he adored, their poverty, their gardens and small pleasures. Short and tender.

read.title: Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio
read.creator: Pu Songling, trans. John Minford
read.why: Nearly five hundred stories of fox spirits, ghosts and scholars, by a man who failed the provincial examination all his life.

read.title: The Scholars
read.creator: Wu Jingzi
read.why: A satirical novel on the examination system and the fools and frauds it produced.

read.title: China’s Last Empire: The Great Qing
read.creator: William T. Rowe
read.why: The best short modern history, which shows the dynasty as a vigorous multi-ethnic empire and not only a decline.

watch.title: The Last Emperor
watch.creator: Bernardo Bertolucci
watch.why: The life of Puyi, who came to the throne at two in 1908 and ended as a gardener in Beijing. The first Western feature filmed in the Forbidden City.

watch.title: Dream of the Red Chamber
watch.creator: China Central Television; Wang Fulin
watch.why: The thirty-six-part series that most Chinese viewers regard as definitive. Costumes, gardens and music were researched for years.

watch.title: The Opium War
watch.creator: Xie Jin
watch.why: A large-scale Chinese film of Lin Zexu’s campaign and the war that followed, made for the return of Hong Kong.

watch.title: Story of Yanxi Palace
watch.creator: Hui Kaidong and Wen Deguang
watch.why: A palace drama of Qianlong’s court. The plot is invention, but the embroidery, hair ornaments and colours are closely copied from surviving objects.

listen.title: Flowing Water
listen.creator: Guan Pinghu, qin
listen.why: An ancient piece for the seven-stringed zither. This recording was sent into space on the Voyager spacecraft in 1977.

listen.title: Ambush from Ten Sides
listen.creator: Traditional, for pipa
listen.why: A battle of 202 BCE told on a four-stringed lute, with drums, horses and the clash of weapons all drawn from the strings.

listen.title: The Peony Pavilion
listen.creator: Tang Xianzu; Kunqu opera
listen.why: The refined southern opera that the court and the literati loved before Peking opera took over. Slow, flute-led and exquisite.

listen.title: The Drunken Concubine
listen.creator: Mei Lanfang, Peking opera
listen.why: Peking opera was formed in the capital from 1790, when troupes came to perform for Qianlong’s eightieth birthday. Mei was its greatest star.

art.title: One Hundred Horses
art.creator: Giuseppe Castiglione, known as Lang Shining
art.why: An eight-metre handscroll by the Italian Jesuit who served three emperors, joining European shading and perspective to Chinese format. In the National Palace Museum, Taipei.

art.title: The Kangxi Emperor’s Southern Inspection Tour
art.creator: Wang Hui and assistants
art.why: Twelve enormous scrolls following the emperor from Beijing to the cities of the south, with every shop and bridge on the way.

art.title: Fish and rocks
art.creator: Bada Shanren
art.why: A prince of the fallen Ming who became a monk and painted birds and fish with a few wet strokes and a sceptical upturned eye.

art.title: The Jadeite Cabbage
art.creator: Palace workshop
art.why: A piece of white and green jade carved into a cabbage with two insects on the leaves. The most visited object in the National Palace Museum, Taipei.

eat.title: Roast duck
eat.creator: Thin slices with pancakes, spring onion and sweet bean sauce
eat.why: A dish of the capital. The restaurant Quanjude, which made the hung-oven method famous, opened in Beijing in 1864.

eat.title: Hot pot
eat.creator: Thin-sliced mutton and vegetables cooked at the table in a copper pot of broth
eat.why: A northern and Manchu favourite. The Qianlong Emperor served hundreds of them at a banquet for the elderly.

eat.title: Sachima
eat.creator: Fried strands of dough bound with honey syrup
eat.why: A Manchu sweet that spread across China with the dynasty.

eat.title: A dish from the Garden of Contentment
eat.creator: Yuan Mei’s recipes
eat.why: The poet Yuan Mei published a book of some three hundred recipes in 1792, with rules such as: do not let the eye or the ear do the eating.

drink.title: Longjing tea
drink.creator: Flat green leaves from Hangzhou
drink.why: The Qianlong Emperor visited the village on his southern tours and, by tradition, named eighteen bushes as his own.

drink.title: Jasmine tea
drink.creator: Green tea scented with fresh blossom
drink.why: The everyday tea of Beijing, drunk from a lidded bowl.

drink.title: Pu’er
drink.creator: Aged, compressed tea from Yunnan
drink.why: Sent to the court as tribute from 1729. The Manchu nobility drank it after rich meat dishes.

customs.title: The examinations
customs.creator: Three days in a cell
customs.why: Candidates were locked into rows of brick cubicles with brush, ink and food, to write essays and poems from memory of the classics. Men sat them into their seventies.

customs.title: Tomb sweeping
customs.creator: At Qingming, in early April
customs.why: Families tidy the graves of their ancestors, set out food and wine, burn paper offerings and picnic beside them.

customs.title: Seals and studio names
customs.creator: A carved stone for a signature
customs.why: A scholar stamped paintings and letters in red with seals bearing his names and mottoes. Collectors added theirs, so a scroll gathered its own history.

customs.title: The queue
customs.creator: Imposed in 1645
customs.why: Han men were ordered to shave the forehead and plait the hair in the Manchu style on pain of death. By 1911 cutting it off was the sign of revolution.

games.title: Weiqi
games.creator: Board game · China
games.why: Go. Black and white stones surround territory on a grid of nineteen lines. The best players of the dynasty, Fan Xiping and Shi Xiangxia, met in a famous series in 1739.

games.title: Mahjong
games.creator: Tile game · China
games.why: Developed from older card games around Ningbo and Shanghai in the late Qing. Four players draw and discard to build sets.

games.title: Xiangqi
games.creator: Board game · China
games.why: Chinese chess, with a river across the board and cannons that jump. Played on every street corner.

games.title: Cricket fighting
games.creator: Autumn pastime · Beijing
games.year: from the Tang, at its height in the Qing
games.why: Male crickets are kept in gourds and clay pots, fed carefully and matched in a small arena. Emperors and porters alike kept them.

festivals.title: Spring Festival
festivals.creator: The first day of the first lunar month, in January or February
festivals.why: The new year. Debts are settled, doors are pasted with red couplets, ancestors are honoured and the family eats together.

festivals.title: Qingming
festivals.creator: 4 or 5 April
festivals.why: Clear and Bright: the day for sweeping the tombs and for the first outing of spring.

festivals.title: Mid-Autumn Festival
festivals.creator: The fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month
festivals.why: Families sit out under the full moon with round cakes and fruit. The court moved to cooler palaces for it.

festivals.title: The Lantern Festival
festivals.creator: The fifteenth day of the first lunar month
festivals.why: The first full moon of the year closes the new year season with lanterns, riddles and sweet rice dumplings.

places.title: The Palace Museum
places.creator: The Forbidden City, Beijing, China
places.why: Nine hundred and eighty buildings behind a moat and red walls. Go past the great halls to the smaller courts and gardens at the back, where the emperors actually lived. Book ahead.

places.title: The Summer Palace
places.creator: Haidian, Beijing, China
places.why: A lake, a hill and a painted corridor nearly a kilometre long, rebuilt by the Empress Dowager Cixi. The marble boat is at the far end.

places.title: The Mountain Resort
places.creator: Chengde, Hebei, China
places.why: The summer capital north of the Wall, where Kangxi and Qianlong hunted and received Mongol and Tibetan leaders. Around it stand temples built in the styles of their lands.

places.title: The classical gardens of Suzhou
places.creator: Jiangsu, China
places.why: The Humble Administrator’s Garden, the Master of the Nets Garden and others: the private worlds of scholar-officials, much altered and tended through the Qing.

places.title: Pingyao
places.creator: Shanxi, China
places.why: A walled town of grey brick courtyards that was the banking centre of the nineteenth-century empire. The first draft bank, founded in 1823, is a museum.

places.title: National Palace Museum
places.creator: Shilin, Taipei, Taiwan
places.why: Much of the imperial collection, moved from Beijing in the 1930s and 1940s: painting, calligraphy, jade and porcelain gathered by the Qing emperors.

ethics.title: Filial devotion
ethics.text: Care for parents in life and remember them in death. The Sacred Edict placed it first.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today that would please your parents, or honour their memory.

ethics.title: Diligence
ethics.text: Zeng Guofan held that every failure in the world comes from laziness, and every success from steady effort.
ethics.practice: Finish the task you least want to do before noon.

ethics.title: Reverence
ethics.text: Be serious and attentive in whatever you do, as if receiving an important guest.
ethics.practice: Do one ordinary thing today with complete care.

ethics.title: Frugality
ethics.text: Live below your means. Great families fall through extravagance within a few generations.
ethics.practice: Go a day without buying anything you do not need.

ethics.title: Restraint in speech
ethics.text: Much talk wastes the breath and makes enemies.
ethics.practice: In one conversation today, listen twice as much as you speak.

ethics.title: Responsibility for the whole
ethics.text: Even a person without office answers for the moral condition of the world.
ethics.practice: Do one small thing for the public good that is nobody’s job.

philosophy.title: Seek truth from facts
philosophy.text: The Qing scholars distrusted grand speculation. Check the text, compare the sources, test the reading. The phrase later became a political slogan.
philosophy.practice: What do you believe that you have never checked?

philosophy.title: Self-cultivation
philosophy.text: The order of the world begins with the ordering of one’s own person. Daily rules, a diary and honest friends are its tools.
philosophy.practice: Write one rule for yourself and keep it for a week.

philosophy.title: The mandate of heaven
philosophy.text: Rule is justified by the welfare of the ruled. A government that lets the people starve has lost its right.
philosophy.practice: By what right does anyone hold authority over you, or you over others?

philosophy.title: Real and unreal
philosophy.text: Cao Xueqin’s novel turns on the thought that wealth, rank and even love are a dream, and that the dream is all we have.
philosophy.practice: What would you grieve to lose that you know cannot last?

philosophy.title: The amateur ideal
philosophy.text: The highest art was made by those who did not do it for a living. Painting and poetry were ways of being a person.
philosophy.practice: Make something today with no thought of selling or showing it.

philosophy.title: Ritual
philosophy.text: Right forms shape right feelings. Bowing teaches respect better than a lecture on it.
philosophy.practice: Perform one courtesy today with full attention to its form.

philosophy.title: Many peoples, one ruler
philosophy.text: The emperor was Confucian sage to the Chinese, khan to the Mongols and a patron of Buddhism to the Tibetans. Empire meant speaking to each in their own terms.
philosophy.practice: To whom do you speak in their language, and whom do you expect to learn yours?

philosophy.title: The closed door
philosophy.text: Confident in its own completeness, the court saw no need of what outsiders offered. The cost of that confidence came due in the next century.
philosophy.practice: What are you sure you have no need to learn?

Which of the rules will you keep?

intro: The Qing was the last of China’s imperial dynasties and the largest. Its rulers were not Chinese. They were Manchus, a people of farmers, hunters and horsemen from the forests north-east of the Great Wall, who organised themselves into military units called banners and, in 1644, were let through the Wall by a Ming general to put down a rebellion. They took the capital and stayed for 268 years.

The conquest was violent. Cities that resisted were sacked, and every Chinese man was ordered to shave his forehead and wear his hair in the Manchu plait, on pain of death. Yet the new rulers also made themselves into model Confucian emperors. Three of them, Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong, reigned in succession for 134 years and were among the ablest monarchs anywhere in the world in their time. They rose before dawn, read the classics, wrote poetry and calligraphy, toured the provinces, read thousands of reports from officials and answered them in their own hand. Under them the empire doubled in size, taking in Mongolia, Tibet, Taiwan and the far west, and the population tripled to some three hundred million.

The country was administered by a remarkably small number of officials, chosen by written examination on the Confucian classics. A boy from almost any family could in theory rise to the highest office through years of study. Few did, but the dream shaped the whole of society. Those who passed even the lower degrees became the local gentry: they settled disputes, ran schools and granaries, compiled genealogies and set the tone of cultivated life. That life centred on the study, with its brush, ink, paper and inkstone, and on a round of reading, writing, tea, gardens, painting, music and the company of friends.

It was also a great age of scholarship and of fiction. Scholars turned from metaphysics to the exact study of ancient texts under the motto seek truth from facts. The emperor Qianlong had every known book copied into a library of thirty-six thousand volumes. And an impoverished descendant of a once grand family, Cao Xueqin, wrote The Story of the Stone, the greatest Chinese novel.

The nineteenth century brought disaster. Population had outrun the land. British merchants forced opium on the country, and when an honest official destroyed their stocks, Britain went to war in 1839 and imposed the first of a series of unequal treaties. A vast rebellion led by a man who believed himself the brother of Jesus cost at least twenty million lives. Reformers such as Zeng Guofan tried to strengthen the state while holding to the old moral discipline. It was not enough. Defeat by Japan in 1895 and the Boxer catastrophe of 1900 discredited the court. The examinations were abolished in 1905, and in 1912 the six-year-old emperor abdicated.

This Onda takes its day from the scholar-official at his best, and in particular from the twelve rules that Zeng Guofan set himself in 1842: rise early, sit quietly, practise the brush, read one book through, record what you learn, guard your speech, walk after meals and keep an honest diary.
guide.origin: Manchuria and Beijing, ruling China, Mongolia, Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan
guide.era: The Manchus took Beijing in 1644. The last emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912

figures.name: Nurhaci
figures.bio: The chieftain who united the Jurchen tribes, created the banner system and had a script made for the Manchu language.

figures.name: The Kangxi Emperor
figures.bio: On the throne for sixty-one years from the age of seven. Hunter, mathematician and patron of learning, who studied geometry with Jesuits and commissioned the standard dictionary of Chinese.

figures.name: The Yongzheng Emperor
figures.bio: A fierce worker who reformed the finances, checked corruption and wrote tens of thousands of comments on reports in red ink, often late into the night.

figures.name: The Qianlong Emperor
figures.bio: Ruler in fact for sixty-three years. Conqueror, collector, author of over forty thousand poems. His last decades were clouded by a corrupt favourite.

figures.name: Gu Yanwu
figures.bio: Scholar who refused to serve the new dynasty and travelled the north on horseback with his books, checking history against the land. A founder of evidential learning.

figures.name: Cao Xueqin
figures.bio: Grandson of a wealthy imperial textile commissioner whose family was ruined. He died poor in the hills west of Beijing with his novel unfinished.

figures.name: Yuan Mei
figures.bio: Poet who retired from office at thirty-two to a garden in Nanjing, taught women students, and wrote on ghosts and on food.

figures.name: Wang Zhenyi
figures.bio: A self-taught astronomer and mathematician who explained eclipses with a lamp, a globe and a mirror, and wrote that daughters can be heroes too.

figures.name: Lin Zexu
figures.bio: The incorruptible commissioner who seized and destroyed twenty thousand chests of British opium at Guangzhou in 1839 and was exiled for it.

figures.name: Zeng Guofan
figures.bio: A scholar from Hunan who raised an army to defeat the Taiping, sponsored the first arsenals and students abroad, and left letters and a diary that became a manual of self-discipline.

figures.name: The Empress Dowager Cixi
figures.bio: A concubine who became regent in 1861 and held power behind the screen for nearly half a century. Her reputation is still being argued over.

figures.name: Puyi
figures.bio: The last emperor. He lost his throne at six, was Japan’s puppet in Manchuria, spent a decade in prison and died a citizen of the People’s Republic.

history.detail: Nurhaci declares a state in the north-east. His son Hong Taiji renames the people Manchu and the dynasty Qing.
A rebel army takes the Ming capital and the last Ming emperor hangs himself. The Manchus enter through the Shanhai Pass and install a boy emperor.
All men are given ten days to adopt the queue. Resistance in the cities of the lower Yangzi is put down with massacres.
He defeats a great revolt in the south, takes Taiwan in 1683, and signs a border treaty with Russia in 1689, the first with a European power.
The empire reaches its greatest extent with the conquest of the far west in the 1750s, at terrible cost to the Dzungar Mongols.
Some 3,500 works are copied by hand into seven sets of the Siku Quanshu. In the same project thousands of books judged hostile are destroyed.
A British mission asks for open trade and a resident ambassador. Qianlong receives it courteously and refuses everything.
After Lin Zexu destroys the opium, British steamships force the Treaty of Nanjing: five ports opened, Hong Kong ceded, an indemnity paid.
A failed examination candidate founds a Heavenly Kingdom at Nanjing. Its suppression is the bloodiest civil war in history.
British and French troops loot and destroy the Garden of Perfect Brightness outside Beijing during the Second Opium War.
Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and others build arsenals, shipyards and schools of translation. Defeat by Japan in 1895 shows how little it has achieved.
A hundred days of reform are crushed by Cixi. Two years later an anti-foreign rising ends with eight armies in the capital.
The system that had chosen China’s officials for thirteen centuries is abolished by decree.
A mutiny at Wuchang on 10 October spreads through the provinces. The emperor’s abdication is signed on 12 February 1912.

concepts.detail: Heaven entrusts rule to a house that governs well and takes it away from one that does not. The Qing claimed to have received it from the failed Ming.
County, provincial and metropolitan tests, held every three years, with success rates of one or two in a hundred. It bound the ambitious of every province to the throne.
A hereditary caste of soldiers and their families, housed in walled quarters of the main cities and paid stipends. They kept the Manchus distinct.
Rigorous philology, epigraphy, geography and mathematics, practised by scholars who suspected that earlier philosophers had read their own ideas into the classics.
Sixteen maxims issued by Kangxi in 1670 on filial duty, thrift, farming, schooling and paying taxes, expounded aloud in every district on the first and fifteenth of the month.
A system by which trusted officials wrote directly and secretly to the emperor, who replied in vermilion ink. It gave the Qing rulers an unmatched view of their empire.
Neighbouring rulers sent envoys with gifts, performed the kowtow and received richer gifts and the right to trade. Europeans did not fit the pattern.
The four accomplishments of a cultivated person, pursued as self-cultivation and not as a trade.

concepts.text: Chinese learning as the base, Western learning for use.
concepts.detail: The late Qing formula for borrowing guns, ships and science while keeping Confucian values intact.

facts.text: Around 1800 the Qing empire held about a third of the world’s people.
The Kangxi Dictionary of 1716 lists more than forty-seven thousand characters and gave its arrangement to every later dictionary.
The Qianlong Emperor abdicated in 1796 so as not to reign longer than his grandfather, and went on ruling in retirement.
The examination compound in Nanjing had more than twenty thousand cells.
Court documents were written in two languages, Manchu and Chinese, and the emperors were expected to be fluent in both.
The blue and white porcelain, silk and tea that Europe craved were paid for in silver, much of it mined in the Americas.

sensitivity.note: This Onda follows the daily discipline of a Qing scholar-official, a small and privileged class. The dynasty they served was a conquest empire, and the culture they lived in is the inheritance of people living today. Take the habits with respect and the history whole.
requiredCaveats: The Qing conquest and its later wars killed very large numbers of people, among them the Dzungar Mongols, who were all but destroyed in the 1750s.
The scholar’s life was open only to men. Women were excluded from the examinations, and many Han women had their feet bound, a practice the Manchus forbade their own daughters.
Zeng Guofan is admired for his self-discipline and also remembered for the severity with which his armies put down the Taiping.
